title: The Workers Who Built the Pyramids
text:
For centuries people imagined the Great Pyramid being raised by vast gangs of slaves under the whip. Herodotus, writing two thousand years after it was built, said a hundred thousand men worked in shifts of three months. Excavations at Giza since the late twentieth century have given a different picture.

title: Joseph Forgives His Brothers
text:
Jacob loved his son Joseph more than his other sons and gave him a richly ornamented robe. Joseph told his brothers about dreams in which they bowed down to him. They hated him for it. One day, far from home, they seized him, threw him into a dry pit, and sold him to traders bound for Egypt. They dipped his robe in goat's blood and let their father believe a wild animal had killed him.

text:
After the Israelites left Egypt, Moses' father-in-law Jethro, a priest of Midian, came to visit him in the wilderness, bringing Moses' wife and sons. The two men greeted each other warmly, and Moses told him everything that had happened.

title: Gilgamesh and Enkidu
text:
Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, was two parts god and one part man, and he was a tyrant. He wore out the young men of the city and took what he wanted, and the people cried out to the gods. So the gods made a match for him: Enkidu, a wild man who lived among the animals on the steppe. Through the woman Shamhat, Enkidu learned to eat bread, drink beer and live among people, and he came to Uruk.

title: Ruth and Naomi
date: ancient Israelite tradition (period of the judges)
text:
During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech of Bethlehem took his wife Naomi and their two sons to the land of Moab. There the sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then Elimelech died, and about ten years later both sons died too. Naomi was left with no husband and no children, only two foreign daughters-in-law.

text:
During the wars with the Philistines, David was at his stronghold near the cave of Adullam, while a Philistine garrison held his home town of Bethlehem and their army was camped in the valley of Rephaim. It was harvest time.

David, homesick and thirsty, spoke a wish aloud: "Oh, that someone would give me a drink of water from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!" It was not an order, only a longing.

date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 10th century BC
text:
Two women came before King Solomon with a baby. They lived together in the same house, and each had given birth to a son, three days apart. There had been no one else in the house.

The first woman told the king what had happened. During the night, the other woman's baby had died, because she had lain on him in her sleep. text:
During the Trojan War, Hector, Troy's greatest warrior, came back from the battlefield into the city. He looked for his wife Andromache at home, but she had gone to the walls with their baby son Astyanax to watch the fighting. He found her near the Scaean Gate.

text:
For ten years the Greeks besieged Troy and could not take it. At last, on the advice of Odysseus, the craftsman Epeius built an enormous wooden horse. The best Greek warriors climbed inside it, and the rest of the army burned their camp and sailed away, though only as far as a nearby island, where they hid.

text: In the 7th century BC, in the state of Qi, two young men named Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya were close friends. Sima Qian preserves Guan Zhong's own memory of that friendship. text:
King Zhuang of Chu, who ruled from 613 to 591 BC, once gave a banquet for his officers that went on into the night. According to the Han dynasty collection Shuo Yuan, compiled by Liu Xiang, a gust of wind blew out the candles. In the darkness one of the guests, drunk, tugged at the clothing of the king's favored lady.

She snatched the tassel off the man's hat and told the king. If he had the lamps relit, she said, he could find the offender by his broken hat and punish him.

text:
Herodotus tells how Solon, the wise lawgiver of Athens, visited Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia. Croesus showed him his treasures and asked who was the happiest man Solon had ever seen, expecting to hear his own name. Solon first named an Athenian, Tellus, who had lived well and died bravely for his city. Croesus then asked who came second. Solon named two young men of Argos, the brothers Cleobis and Biton.

title: The Ass Carrying the Image
text:
A donkey was given an important job. It was to carry a famous wooden statue of a god through the streets of a city to the temple where the image would be installed.

As the procession passed, crowds lined the streets. People bowed low, knelt and pressed their hands together in reverence. The donkey looked around and drew its own conclusion: all this respect was for him. title: The Bundle of Sticks
text:
An old farmer had several sons who could not stop quarreling. They argued over the work, over the land and over every small slight, and nothing he said made any difference. He had pleaded with them and scolded them, and still the house was full of their bickering.

title: The Dog and Its Reflection
text:
A dog had got hold of a fine piece of meat, perhaps from a butcher's shop, and was carrying it home in his mouth to eat in peace. On the way he had to cross a narrow plank laid over a stream.

Halfway across he glanced down at the water. There below him he saw another dog, holding another piece of meat in its jaws, and to his eyes that piece looked twice as big as his own.

title: The Farmer and the Viper
text:
One bitter winter day a farmer was walking home across his frozen fields when he saw a snake lying on the ground, stiff and almost dead from the cold.

He knew perfectly well what kind of snake it was. Even so he felt sorry for it. He picked it up, opened his coat and put it against his chest to warm it with his own body, and carried it home.

text:
A crow found a piece of cheese, or in older versions a piece of meat, and flew up to a branch to eat it in peace. A fox passing below caught the smell and stopped. He wanted that cheese, and he knew he could not climb the tree to take it.

text:
A fox was caught in a trap. He struggled and twisted and finally tore himself free, but he left his fine bushy tail behind in the iron jaws. When he limped home, he realized how ridiculous he looked, and he dreaded the laughter of the other foxes.

title: The Horse and the Overloaded Ass
text:
A man set out on a journey with a horse and an ass. He put the whole load on the ass, and the horse trotted along carrying nothing at all.

The ass struggled under the weight. After a while he begged the horse to take part of the load. It would be nothing much for you, he said, and it might save my life. The horse refused. The load was not his business, and he had no intention of tiring himself.

title: The Lion and the Boar
text:
It was a scorching summer day, and every animal was desperate for water. A lion and a boar reached a small spring at exactly the same moment. Neither would let the other drink first. They argued, then charged, and soon they were locked in a savage fight, tearing at each other with claws and tusks.

text:
The North Wind and the Sun once argued about which of them was the stronger. Neither would give way, so they agreed on a test. A traveler was walking along the road below, wrapped in a cloak. Whoever could make him take it off would be the winner.

title: The Thief and His Mother
text:
A schoolboy stole a writing tablet from a classmate and carried it home to his mother. She did not punish him or send him back with it. Instead she praised him for his cleverness.

Encouraged, he next brought home a cloak he had taken, and again she approved. As he grew into a young man his thefts grew with him, from small things to things of real value, until at last he was caught in the act. His hands were bound behind his back and he was led away to be executed.

text:
Two men were walking together along a road. One of them spotted an axe lying in the dust, picked it up, and called out happily, "I have found an axe!"

His companion corrected him. Since they were traveling together, he said, it would be better to say that we have found an axe. The first man shrugged and kept the axe for himself.

text:
Sima Qian tells how Sun Wu, known as Sun Tzu, a native of Qi, came to King Helu of Wu with his thirteen chapters on the art of war. The king said he had read them all and asked whether Sun Wu could give a small test of his methods, using women. Sun Wu agreed.

text:
Confucius once visited the ancestral temple of Duke Huan of Lu and noticed a strange vessel set at an angle. He asked the temple keeper what it was. The keeper told him it was a vessel kept at the right side of the seat as a warning.

location: Yue and Wu (modern Zhejiang and Jiangsu, China)
text:
In 494 BC King Gou Jian of Yue was crushed by King Fu Chai of Wu and trapped with his last troops on Mount Kuaiji. On the advice of his ministers he surrendered, and according to tradition he and his wife went to Wu to serve its king in humiliation before being allowed to return home. title: Aristides Writes His Own Name
text:
In classical Athens citizens could vote once a year to send one prominent man into exile for ten years. Each voter scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery, an ostrakon. Around 482 BC the vote turned against Aristides, a statesman so famous for his honesty that he was called "the Just".

date: Ancient Jewish tradition, set in the 5th century BC
text:
Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, had become queen to Ahasuerus, king of Persia, without revealing her people. Then the king's chief minister Haman, enraged that Mordecai would not bow to him, obtained a royal decree to destroy all the Jews of the empire on a single day.

location: Jeta's Grove, Savatthi (modern Uttar Pradesh, India)
text:
A monk named Malunkyaputta was troubled because the Buddha had never answered certain great questions. Was the world eternal or not? Was it finite or infinite? Were the soul and the body the same thing or different? Did an enlightened one exist after death or not? text:
Some monks came to the Buddha after their alms round in Savatthi. They had seen teachers of rival sects arguing in the town, each insisting that his own view was the only truth and wounding the others with sharp words. The Buddha answered with a story.

location: Ying, capital of Chu (modern Hubei, China)
text:
In the 5th century BC the master craftsman Gongshu Ban built new siege ladders, called cloud ladders, for the powerful state of Chu, which planned to use them against the small state of Song. The philosopher Mozi, who taught universal love and opposed wars of aggression, heard of it. The book that bears his name says he set out at once and walked ten days and ten nights to the Chu capital.

text:
The legendary physician Bian Que came to see Duke Huan of Cai. After standing before him for a while, he said: "My lord, you have an illness in the skin. If it is not treated, it will go deeper." The duke replied that he was perfectly well. When Bian Que left, the duke remarked that doctors like to treat healthy people so they can take credit for curing them.

date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD
text:
King Dasharatha of Ayodhya, growing old, decided to crown his eldest son Rama as heir. The city rejoiced. But his young queen Kaikeyi, stirred up by her maid Manthara, reminded the king of two boons he had promised her long ago when she saved his life in battle.

text:
In 394 BC, according to Roman tradition, the general Marcus Furius Camillus was besieging Falerii, a town of the Faliscans north of Rome. The siege was dragging on, and the town was well defended.

Livy and Plutarch tell the story. The Faliscans entrusted the education of the children of their leading families to a schoolmaster, who took them out of the town each day for walks and exercise. text:
Epaminondas was the Theban general who broke Sparta's military power at Leuctra in 371 BC and became one of the most admired men in Greece. He also had enemies at home in Thebes who resented his influence.

text:
In the state of Qi in the 4th century BC, the general Tian Ji often raced horses against King Wei and the princes for large wagers. Each side entered three horses, one from each of three grades: top, middle and lowest. The king's horses in each grade were a little better than Tian Ji's, so Tian Ji kept losing.

text:
Years after his rival Pang Juan had him mutilated, Sun Bin faced him again. In about 342 BC the state of Wei attacked Han, and Qi sent an army under Tian Ji with Sun Bin as strategist. As before, they marched toward the Wei capital, and Pang Juan turned back to chase them.

text:
In 326 BC Alexander the Great crossed the Hydaspes River in the Punjab and met the army of the Indian king Porus. It was one of Alexander's hardest battles. Porus fought from a huge war elephant at the center of his line and kept fighting after his army had broken, though badly wounded.

text:
King Hui of Liang told Mencius that he did his utmost for his people. When famine struck the region inside the river bend, he moved people to the east bank and sent grain to those who stayed, and when it struck the east he did the same in reverse. None of the neighboring rulers took such care. Yet their populations did not shrink and his did not grow. Why?

text:
King Zhao of Yan came to the throne of a state that had just been ravaged by its neighbor Qi. He wanted to attract able men to help him rebuild and take revenge, and he asked the scholar Guo Wei how to do it. Guo Wei answered with a story.

text:
A frog lived in an old, broken down well. One day a great turtle from the Eastern Sea passed by, and the frog called up to him, delighted to show off his home.

location: States of Zhao and Yan, Ancient China
text:

text:
Zhuang Xin, a minister of Chu, warned King Xiang that the court was in danger. The king surrounded himself with flattering favorites, lived in luxury and ignored the affairs of state, while the powerful state of Qin was watching. If this went on, Zhuang Xin said, Chu would fall.

text:
The king of Benares loved hunting deer so much that he forced his subjects to leave their fields to drive game for him. To free themselves, the people built a great enclosure in the royal park and herded two whole herds of deer into it. One herd was led by the Banyan Deer, the future Buddha, and the other by the Branch Deer. The king spared both leaders but hunted the rest, and many deer were wounded in the chase.

text:
In this Jataka tale the future Buddha was born as the king of a troop of eighty thousand monkeys. They lived in a great mango tree on the bank of the Ganges, whose fruit was so sweet that the monkey king had them strip every mango from the branches over the water, so none would float downstream and reveal the tree to men. date: c. 4th century BC to 4th century AD
text:
A man in ancient China lost his axe and could not find it anywhere. He began to suspect his neighbor's son.

Once the thought had come to him, he watched the boy closely. The way the boy walked looked like the walk of a man who had stolen an axe. His expression looked like the expression of a man who had stolen an axe. The way he spoke sounded exactly like the way a thief speaks. text:
In 217 BC Hannibal destroyed a Roman army at Lake Trasimene, and Rome in panic named Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator. Fabius decided not to fight Hannibal in open battle at all. Instead he followed the Carthaginian army along the hills, camping on high ground, cutting off foragers and stragglers, and denying Hannibal the decisive victory he needed. text:
In 209 BC the young Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio captured New Carthage, the Carthaginian base in Spain. Among the prisoners, Livy says, his soldiers brought him a young woman of extraordinary beauty.

text:

location: From Chang'an (modern Xi'an, China) to Central Asia
text:
Around 138 BC Emperor Wu of Han wanted allies against the Xiongnu, the nomadic empire that raided China's northern frontier. He had heard that a people called the Yuezhi, driven west by the Xiongnu, wanted revenge. He asked for volunteers to find them. Zhang Qian, a palace official, set out with more than a hundred men and a guide named Ganfu.

text:
The Talmud tells that Honi the Circle Maker was troubled by a verse in the Psalms about the return from exile: "We were like dreamers." Seventy years of exile, he wondered; can a person really dream for seventy years?

One day, walking along the road, he saw a man planting a carob tree. Honi asked him how long it would take for the tree to bear fruit. "Seventy years," the man said. Honi asked whether he really expected to live seventy years to eat from it.

text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, orator and statesman, loved his daughter Tullia more than anyone. His letters call her his darling and his delight. Her marriages were unlucky. Her third husband, Dolabella, was unfaithful and spendthrift, and they divorced. In January 45 BC she gave birth to a son, and a month later, in February, she died at Cicero's villa at Tusculum.

text:
Julia was the only child of the emperor Augustus. He used her as a tool of dynastic policy. At fourteen she was married to her cousin Marcellus, who died two years later. Then she was married to Agrippa, Augustus's closest general, a man a generation older, and bore him five children. When Agrippa died, Augustus made his stepson Tiberius divorce a wife he loved in order to marry Julia. The marriage was unhappy, and Tiberius withdrew to Rhodes.

text:
Drona was the great teacher of archery to the princes of the Kuru royal house, and Arjuna was his favorite pupil. Drona had promised Arjuna that no archer in the world would ever be his equal.

One day a young man named Ekalavya, the son of a chief of the Nishadas, a forest tribe, came and asked to be Drona's student. Drona refused him because of his low birth. text:
A hungry jackal named Chandarava wandered into a town looking for food. The town dogs chased him, and in his panic he leapt into a large vat of indigo dye in a dyer's yard. When he crawled out and escaped into the forest, his fur was a deep, strange blue.

text:
A pair of crows lived in a great tree. Every time they hatched chicks, a black serpent that lived in a hollow at the foot of the tree climbed up and ate them. The crows grieved but were too small to fight a snake.

They went to their friend, a jackal, for advice. The jackal told them that what could not be done by force could be done by cleverness. He told them where to find a weapon.

text:
An old heron lived beside a pond full of fish. He had grown too old and slow to catch them easily, so he thought of a trick. He stood at the edge of the water looking miserable and refused to eat.

A crab asked him what was wrong. The heron said he had heard terrible news: fishermen were coming soon to drain the pond and catch everything in it. He was sad because he would lose his food and his neighbors would die.

text:
In a town there lived four young brahmins who were close friends. Three of them had studied for years and mastered many learned sciences, but they had little common sense. The fourth had no great learning, but he had plenty of sense. They decided to travel together to seek their fortune with their knowledge.

In a pond lived three large fish. One was called Forethought, one Ready Wit, and one Whatever Will Be.

One evening some fishermen walked past the pond and stopped to look at it. It was full of fish, they said, and the water was low. Tomorrow they would come back with their nets and catch the lot.

text:
At the end of their lives, after the great war and many years of rule, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi gave up their kingdom and set out on a final journey toward the Himalayas, heading for the mountain of the gods. A dog joined them at the start and followed them all the way.

text:
Daedalus, the great craftsman of Athens, was trapped on Crete by King Minos, who would not let him leave. Land and sea were guarded, but the sky was not. So Daedalus set to work making wings. He laid feathers in rows from small to large, tied them with thread at the middle and fixed them with wax at the base, and bent them gently to curve like a bird's.

date: Greek myth; Ovid 8 AD, Plutarch c. 100 AD
text:
King Minos of Crete had defeated Athens and demanded a cruel tribute: every few years the Athenians had to send seven young men and seven young women to Crete. There they were sent into the Labyrinth, the vast maze built by the craftsman Daedalus, where the Minotaur, a monster with the body of a man and the head of a bull, lived. None ever came out.

text:

During the meal, Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer garment and tied a towel around his waist. He poured water into a basin and began to wash his disciples' feet and dry them with the towel.

text:

text:
Peter asked Jesus how often he should forgive someone who wronged him. As many as seven times? Not seven times, Jesus said, but seventy-seven times, and he told a story.

A king decided to settle accounts with his servants. One of them owed him ten thousand talents, a sum so vast he could never repay it. text:
Some bees had built their honeycombs high in an oak tree. A group of lazy drones came along and claimed the combs were theirs. The bees protested, and since neither side would give way, the case was brought before a judge: the wasp.

text:
During the Roman siege of Jerusalem around 70 AD, the city was controlled by zealot factions determined to fight to the end. The Babylonian Talmud tells a story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the leading sage of the time, who believed the city could not hold.

text:
Ban Biao, a scholar of the first century AD, began writing a continuation of Sima Qian's great history of China. When he died, his son Ban Gu took over and reshaped the work into a history of the Former Han dynasty, the Book of Han. Ban Gu's twin brother, Ban Chao, became a famous general in Central Asia. Their younger sister, Ban Zhao, was married at fourteen, widowed young, and devoted herself to study.

text:

date: 2nd century AD (set in the 1st century AD)
text:
The Roman writer Aulus Gellius retold this story from the scholar Apion, who claimed to have seen its ending in Rome. A slave named Androcles ran away from a cruel master, a Roman official in Africa. He hid in a desert cave, and soon a lion limped in, groaning, and held out a swollen paw. Androcles found a large thorn buried in it, pulled it out, pressed out the pus and bound the wound.

text:
In the late 160s the Roman Empire was in crisis. A plague brought back by the army from the east was killing large numbers of people, and Germanic peoples were crossing the Danube frontier. The emperor Marcus Aurelius needed money for a long war, and the treasury was empty.

text:
The Talmud records a conversation between the Roman Antoninus and Rabbi Judah the Prince. Antoninus argued that body and soul could each escape judgment. The body could say that it was the soul that sinned, since once the soul left, the body lay still like a stone. text:
One of the most famous stories of the Three Kingdoms is a bluff. The oldest version survives because the historian Pei Songzhi, in the 5th century, quoted it in his commentary on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, attributing it to an earlier writer, Guo Chong.

text:
In 390 a riot broke out in Thessalonica, in Greece, and the crowd killed Butheric, the commander of the local garrison. The emperor Theodosius I, furious, ordered a reprisal. Soldiers trapped the people of the city in the circus and massacred them. Theodoret, a church historian of the next century, puts the dead at seven thousand.

text:
In the early sixth century, Benedict of Nursia, an Italian who had once lived as a hermit, founded a monastery at Monte Cassino, south of Rome. Around 530 to 540 he wrote a short rule, in 73 chapters, to govern the daily life of his monks. He called it "a little rule for beginners."

text:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid was a wealthy merchant of Mecca. According to the early biography of Ibn Ishaq, she hired a young man named Muhammad to take her goods to Syria, was impressed by his honesty, and proposed marriage to him herself. Tradition says he was twenty-five and she was about forty.

text:
Among the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad collected by al-Bukhari is a short story about a woman of the Children of Israel. She was a prostitute, the kind of person respectable people looked down on.

One hot day she came upon a dog walking around and around a well. Its tongue was hanging out and it was so close to dying of thirst that it was licking the damp earth. There was no bucket, and the water lay far below.

text:
In 637 or 638 Jerusalem surrendered to the Arab armies after a long siege. The Patriarch Sophronius is said to have insisted on surrendering only to the caliph himself, so Umar ibn al-Khattab traveled from Medina to accept the city. Muslim and Christian traditions agree that he came simply dressed and that the city was taken without a sack.

text:
Around 797 Charlemagne, king of the Franks, sent an embassy to Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, ruler of the richest empire of the age. The mission included two Frankish nobles and a Jewish merchant named Isaac, probably chosen for his languages and knowledge of the routes. The journey took years. Both noblemen died along the way.

text:
In January 878 the Danish army under Guthrum made a surprise attack on Chippenham, where Alfred, king of Wessex, was spending the winter. Most of Wessex submitted to the Danes. Alfred escaped with a small band and hid in the marshes of Somerset, at a place called Athelney. For a few months the last independent English king was a fugitive.

text:
An old man died and left seventeen camels to his three sons. His will said that the eldest should have half of the camels, the second son a third, and the youngest a ninth.

text:
The great hero Rostam, hunting near the borders of Turan, lost his horse Rakhsh and followed its tracks to the city of Samangan. text:
In 1076 the struggle between the young German king Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops came to a head. Henry and his bishops declared the pope deposed. Gregory answered by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oaths of loyalty.

text:
Yue Fei was a general of the Southern Song dynasty who fought the Jurchen Jin invaders who had overrun northern China in the 1120s. He rose from a poor farming family to command one of the most effective armies of the age, and won a series of victories that brought him close to recovering lost territory.

text:
An old tiger lived beside a lake. He had become too weak to hunt, so he sat on the bank after bathing, holding a gold bracelet in his paw, and called out to passing travelers that he would give it away as an act of charity.

A traveler heard him and was tempted, but he was not a fool. It was a fine bracelet, but its owner was a tiger. He asked how he could trust a creature that killed people.

text:
Henry II of England ruled an empire stretching from Scotland's border to the Pyrenees, much of it through his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine. They had four sons who survived to adulthood. When King Uther Pendragon died, he left no acknowledged heir, and the barons of Britain could not agree who should rule. At Christmas they gathered in the church in the great city to pray for a sign. When they came out after Mass, they found a block of stone with an anvil on it, and a sword stuck through the anvil. When Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206, he united steppe peoples who had spent generations raiding and betraying each other. To hold them together, he reorganized his whole people on a decimal system.

That autumn a wandering dervish in his sixties arrived in the city: Shams-i Tabrizi, a restless, outspoken mystic who had spent his life searching for a companion who could bear his company.

In the Ramayana, Rama's army of monkeys and bears built a bridge across the sea to Lanka to rescue Sita. A story told across India adds a small figure to that great work.

text:
Afonso I, called Nzinga Mbemba before his baptism, ruled the Kingdom of Kongo in west central Africa from about 1509 to the early 1540s. Thomas More was a lawyer, scholar and author of Utopia, and from 1529 he was Lord Chancellor of England, the highest office under the king. When Henry VIII broke with the pope to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and marry Anne Boleyn, More could not agree. In 1532 he resigned and retired into private life.
